who: Dallas Bed Rest and Training Study · Circulation, 1968 and 2001
quote: In 1966, five healthy 20-year-old men spent 3 weeks in bed, which ‘had a more profound impact on physical work capacity than did 3 decades of aging.’ At 50, six months of training reversed their age-related loss of aerobic power.
meaning: Three weeks in bed hurt their fitness more than 30 years of ageing. Training at 50 won it back.

who: J. N. Morris et al. · The Lancet, 1953; Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1994
quote: In 1953 Dr Jerry Morris found London bus conductors, who climbed the double-decker stairs, had less heart disease than drivers, who sat at the wheel. In 1994 he wrote that physical activity ‘could be today's "best buy" in public health...’
meaning: The bus workers who climbed stairs all day had healthier hearts than the drivers who sat.

who: R. S. Paffenbarger Jr. et al. · New England Journal of Medicine, 1986
quote: Of 16,936 Harvard alumni, men who burned 2,000+ kcal a week walking, climbing stairs and playing sport had death rates ‘one quarter to one third lower’ than less active men. The study's leader, Ralph Paffenbarger, began running at 45.
meaning: Men who walked, climbed stairs and played sport lived longer. The scientist himself began running at 45.

who: C. P. Wen et al. · The Lancet, 2011
quote: A study of 416,175 adults in Taiwan (1996-2008) found that people who exercised about 15 minutes a day (92 minutes a week) had a 14% lower risk of death and a 3-year longer life expectancy than inactive people.
meaning: Even about 15 minutes of exercise a day was linked to a longer life.

who: D. A. Bennett et al., China Kadoorie Biobank · JAMA Cardiology, 2017
quote: China Kadoorie Biobank: 487,334 adults aged 30 to 79 in 10 areas of China. About one more hour of brisk walking a day went with a 6% lower risk of major heart and blood-vessel disease.
meaning: In China, people who moved more each day had less heart and blood-vessel disease.

who: X. R. Pan et al., Da Qing study · Diabetes Care, 1997
quote: In 1986, clinics in Da Qing, China, screened 110,660 people and found 577 with raised blood sugar. After 6 years, 41.1% of the exercise group had developed diabetes, against 67.7% of the control group.
meaning: For people with high blood sugar, exercise lowered the chance of getting diabetes.

who: F. Li et al. · JAMA Internal Medicine, 2018
quote: 670 people aged 70 or older, who had fallen in the past year or were slow to get up and walk, took two one-hour classes a week for 24 weeks. The 224 doing tai chi had 152 falls; the 223 stretching had 363.
meaning: A special tai chi class helped older people keep their balance and fall far less.

who: M. A. Fiatarone et al. · JAMA, 1990
quote: Ten frail nursing-home residents aged about 90 did 8 weeks of strength training. The 9 who finished got on average 174% stronger and walked 48% faster.
meaning: Even at 90, muscles grow stronger when you train them.

who: N. R. Lazarus · NPR, 2018; Aging Cell, 2018
quote: At 82, Professor Norman Lazarus still cycled: ‘...I wasn't aging in the way that I'd sort of been taught in medical school.’ In his study, cyclists aged 55-79 had as many new T cells as young adults.
meaning: People who kept cycling for years kept parts of their immune system young.

quote: A mountain of evidence suggests that the Fountain of Youth runs with sweat. That sweat, moreover, needs to keep flowing as we age.
meaning: Moving and sweating help keep you young. Keep doing it as you grow older.
